docs.title: bixverse
docs.text: Streams a bixverse binary cell-major store into minibatches for neural network training. The Rust crate does the work: a feeder thread decompresses and materialises batches ahead of your training step, and the GIL is released while it does. No materialising the experiment in memory, no Python-side decode.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
uv pip install bixverse            # numpy only
uv pip install "bixverse[sparse]"  # adds scipy, for Batch.scipy_csr
uv pip install "bixverse[torch]"   # torch, for bixverse.nn
uv pip install "bixverse[mlx]"     # MLX, Apple Silicon only

docs.title: Thirty seconds
docs.text:
import bixverse as bv

reader = bv.CellReader("counts.bin")
loader = bv.CellLoader(reader, batch_size=256, layer="norm", seed=42)

for batch in loader:
    x = batch.scipy_csr()  # (256, n_genes) CSR

Cell-major stores only. A gene-major file raises on construction.

Next: the quickstart, then the API reference.

docs.title: Open a store
docs.text:
import bixverse as bv

reader = bv.CellReader("counts.bin")
reader.total_cells
reader.total_genes

docs.title: Iterate batches
docs.text:
loader = bv.CellLoader(reader, batch_size=256, layer="norm", seed=42)

for batch in loader:
    x = batch.scipy_csr()

Each pass over a loader reshuffles and spawns its own feeder thread, so two concurrent passes don't share state. The seed is mixed with the epoch counter: same seed means the same sequence of epochs, not the same epoch twice.

docs.title: Train and validation splits
docs.text:
Hand the loader an index array to iterate a subset:

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
perm = rng.permutation(reader.total_cells)
train = bv.CellLoader(reader, perm[:180_000], batch_size=256)
val = bv.CellLoader(reader, perm[180_000:], batch_size=256, shuffle=False)

docs.title: Subset or reorder genes
docs.text:
genes= takes store gene indices, in the column order you want. Repeats raise.

loader = bv.CellLoader(reader, batch_size=256, genes=hvg_indices)

docs.title: Batches
docs.text:
A Batch is a NamedTuple of (raw, norm, indices, indptr, shape, cell_ids). The layer you didn't ask for is None. cell_ids is the store index of each row, which is how per-cell covariates get joined back on.

Field Sparse Dense raw / norm CSR-ordered float32 (n_cells, n_genes) float32 indices / indptr uint32 CSR components None shape (n_cells, n_genes) same cell_ids store index per row same

batch.values() returns the single requested layer. batch.scipy_csr() rebuilds a scipy.sparse.csr_matrix sharing the same buffers.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text: "raw" gives the counts. "norm" gives log1p(count / library_size * target_size), computed at write time and stored as float16, so expect agreement with a recomputation to about three decimal places. "both" returns the two together over one sparsity pattern.

docs.title: Sparse by default
docs.text: sparse=True is the default and you want it. A dense batch pays a zero-fill and a scatter over batch_size * n_genes floats however few counts it holds. At droplet sparsity that's roughly twenty times the memory traffic, on the feeder thread, every batch. Build the dense tensor on the GPU if you need one. Pass sparse=False only when you have to.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Ctrl-C can't interrupt a batch mid-decode: the GIL is released while the feeder works, and Python signal handlers only run while it's held.
  • The store is memory-mapped and the reader hints random access. Right for a shuffled loader, wrong for a sequential full scan.

docs.title: scVI
docs.text:
bixverse.nn carries a barebone scVI (Lopez et al., Nature Methods, 2018) for batch correction. It trains straight off a bixverse store: counts stream through the Rust loader, so there's no AnnData, no Lightning and no registry in the way. Two backends, torch (cuda, mps or cpu) and MLX on Apple Silicon, with the same network on both.

pip install "bixverse[torch]"   # or bixverse[mlx] on Apple Silicon

docs.title: Train and embed
docs.text:
You hand it the store, the cells to use, the genes to model and one batch label per cell. Indices are the store's own, 0-based.

import numpy as np
import bixverse.nn as bvnn

store = "counts_cells.bin"
cells = np.array([...])  # store cell indices, e.g. the QC survivors
hvg = np.array([...])  # store gene indices, e.g. 2000 HVGs
batch = np.array([...])  # one label per entry of `cells`

fit = bvnn.train_scvi(store, cells, hvg, batch, backend="torch", seed=42)
latent = bvnn.scvi_latent(fit, store, cells, batch)  # (n_cells, 10)

latent comes back in the order of cells, and is the posterior mean of z, same as scvi-tools' get_latent_representation(). Feed it to whatever builds your kNN graph.

Want a held-out score? Train on a subset of the cells and score the rest:

bvnn.scvi_elbo(fit, store, test_cells, test_batch)
# {'elbo': ..., 'reconstruction': ..., 'kl': ...}, means per cell

docs.title: What's in, what's out
docs.text:
The defaults are scvi-tools 1.5.1's SCVI plus its TrainingPlan: ZINB likelihood (NB via ScviParams(gene_likelihood="nb")), observed library size, gene-wise dispersion, one hidden layer of 128, a 10-d latent, batch one-hot into every decoder layer with the encoder blind to batch, Adam with lr 1e-3, eps 0.01 and weight decay 1e-6, batch size 128, KL warmup over 400 epochs and scvi-tools' epoch heuristic (min(round(20000 / n_cells * 400), 400)).

Not there, and not coming until something asks for it: Poisson and Gaussian likelihoods, learned library size, batch-, label- or cell-wise dispersion, extra covariates, labels (so no scANVI), minified data and scArches surgery.

Library size is the sum over the genes you pass, like scvi-tools on an HVG AnnData. A cell with no counts over those genes raises rather than training on log(0).

docs.title: How close is it to scvi-tools?
docs.text:
Two levels of check.

Same weights, same answer. The tests load a trained scvi-tools 1.5.1 module into ours, run both on one batch with z at the posterior mean, and compare. The encoder mean, reconstruction term and KL agree to rtol = 1e-5, for NB and ZINB. Our torch weights then go into the MLX model and agree to 1e-4 (MLX has no lgamma, so it uses a Lanczos approximation).

Same training, same kind of result. On the two PBMC batches from the bixverse batch correction vignette (5841 cells after QC, 2000 HVGs, 90/10 split, three seeds each, M1 Max), each arm trains on the same 5257 cells:

arm device train, s held-out ELBO kBET accept iLISI scvi-tools SCVI cpu 243 754.8 0.645 1.475 scvi-tools SCVI mps 170 754.5 0.653 1.484 bixverse torch cpu 220 754.7 0.636 1.476 bixverse torch mps 74 753.6 0.650 1.484 bixverse MLX gpu 31 753.9 0.623 1.463 uncorrected PCA 0.013 1.013 Harmony 0.857 1.621

Means over three seeds. Held-out ELBO is the per-cell negative ELBO on the 584 held-out cells, every arm scored by the same code (scvi-tools weights loaded into ours); its seed-to-seed range is about 2. kBET and iLISI come from bixverse's calculate_integration_metrics_sc and calculate_lisi_sc. The network is the same on both sides, so the MPS gap sits outside the maths: mostly torch.distributions argument checks that stall the GPU queue every step, plus Lightning's per-step bookkeeping. Data loading costs the same on both sides.

VAE latents aren't identifiable, so two seeds of scvi-tools already disagree with each other. The fair comparison is ours against scvi-tools, read against scvi-tools against itself:

pair (scvi-tools on cpu) Procrustes disparity kNN Jaccard (k = 15) Leiden ARI scvi-tools vs scvi-tools 0.470 0.085 0.689 bixverse torch (mps) vs scvi-tools 0.463 0.085 0.683 bixverse torch (cpu) vs scvi-tools 0.482 0.082 0.690 bixverse MLX vs scvi-tools 0.472 0.085 0.683

Means over all pairs of runs, three seeds a side.

Ours sits inside scvi-tools' own seed-to-seed spread on every measure. A Procrustes disparity near 0.47 between two runs of the same code is also the reason a small Procrustes delta is the wrong thing to ask for.

scvi-tools' own mlxSCVI is a different network (two hidden layers, BatchNorm momentum 0.9, NB or Poisson only), so it's not a port of SCVI and doesn't land on the same embedding. It integrates harder on these two batches.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• scvi-tools' accelerator="auto" ignores MPS. Ask for "mps" explicitly if you benchmark against it.
  • The MLX backend compiles its training step with mx.compile. On this data that took 400 epochs from 82 s to 50 s.
  • torch.compile isn't used. On MPS it cut compute from 0.175 s to 0.136 s per epoch but costs about 5 s up front, and the inductor backend there is still experimental.
  • There's no torch DataLoader in the loop: the Rust feeder thread already decodes ahead of the training step.

docs.title: CellLoader
docs.text:
CellLoader(
    reader: CellReader,
    indices: Any = None,
    *,
    batch_size: int = 256,
    shuffle: bool = True,
    seed: int | None = None,
    layer: Layer = "norm",
    sparse: bool = True,
    prefetch: int = 4,
    drop_last: bool = False,
    genes: Any = None,
)

Iterate a cell-major store in minibatches, decoding ahead of the consumer.

Each pass spawns one feeder thread that decompresses and materialises batches into a bounded queue, so decode overlaps the training step. The queue depth is the backpressure knob, not a parallelism knob: decode is already rayon-parallel inside a single batch.

>>> import bixverse as bv
>>> reader = bv.CellReader("counts.bin")
>>> loader = bv.CellLoader(reader, batch_size=256)
>>> for batch in loader:
...     x = batch.scipy_csr()

Sparse is the default. A dense batch costs a zero-fill and a scatter over batch_size * n_genes floats no matter how few non-zeros it holds, which at droplet sparsity is roughly twenty times the memory traffic.

Build a loader.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default reader CellReader

An open cell-major CellReader.

required indices Any

Cells to iterate. None uses every cell in the store.

None batch_size int

Cells per batch.

256 shuffle bool

Reshuffle at the start of every epoch.

True seed int | None

Base seed for the shuffle. None draws one at random.

None layer Layer

"raw", "norm" or "both".

'norm' sparse bool

CSR components when true, a dense buffer when false.

True prefetch int

Batches held in flight by the feeder thread.

4 drop_last bool

Drop a trailing partial batch.

False genes Any

Store gene indices to keep, in the column order wanted. None keeps every gene.

None

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

For a gene-major store, an unusable parameter, an out-of-range cell or gene index, or a repeated gene.

docs.title: nn
docs.text:
Neural network models trained straight off a bixverse store.

scVI (Lopez et al., 2018) for batch correction, on torch or on MLX. Counts stream from the store through the Rust loader; nothing goes through AnnData. Importing this module needs neither framework; training on one needs its extra, bixverse[torch] or bixverse[mlx].

>>> import bixverse.nn as bvnn
>>> fit = bvnn.train_scvi("counts_cells.bin", cells, hvg, batch)
>>> latent = bvnn.scvi_latent(fit, "counts_cells.bin", cells, batch)

docs.title: bixverse
docs.text:
Single-cell streaming for Python, in Rust.

Opens a bixverse binary sparse store and yields minibatches fast enough to keep a GPU training loop fed. The decode never leaves Rust: a feeder thread decompresses and materialises batches ahead of the consumer, releasing the GIL while it works.

>>> import bixverse as bv
>>> reader = bv.CellReader("counts.bin")
>>> loader = bv.CellLoader(reader, batch_size=256, layer="norm")
>>> for batch in loader:
...     x = batch.scipy_csr()

Batches are sparse CSR by default. Pass sparse=False for a dense (batch_size, n_genes) array, and expect it to cost a zero-fill and a scatter over every gene whether or not it holds a count.
